On the Encoding of Calendar Features in Covariate-Informed Time Series Foundation Models

Alexander Kreusel ††thanks: Equal contribution.    Maximilian Beichter11footnotemark: 1    Alexandra Nikoltchovska Affiliation: Benjamin Schäfer, Ralf Mikut, Frederik Zahn, Veit Hagenmeyer Affiliation: Institute for Automation and Applied Informatics Affiliation: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology Affiliation: Karlsruhe, Germany Email: {firstname.lastname}@kit.edu
Abstract

Time series foundation models (TSFMs) increasingly offer covariate support, with calendar information being the most common type of categorical covariate in practice, as it is available for every point in time. However, how these features are encoded is largely treated as an implementation detail rather than as an object of study, despite encoding being one of the few design choices left for pretrained models at inference time. With the present study, we demonstrate that the way information is propagated into the model substantially affects forecast accuracy of TSFMs. Therefore, we systematically compare seven calendar encodings, including three conventional target-agnostic representations (ordinal, one-hot, and cyclic) and four target encodings, across four state-of-the-art TSFMs (Chronos-2, TabPFN-TS-3, TiRex-2, TimesFM-3)11 1 Results of t0t_{0}-beta Meyer et al. (2026a) are in preparation. on nine datasets from multiple domains in a zero-shot rolling evaluation. The nine datasets are influenced by social activities, such as weekends and holidays, making calendar information particularly relevant for forecasting. We find that encoding choice affects forecast accuracy across all models, with MASE differences of up to 9.9 % on non-holidays and 83 % on holidays within a single model. Effectiveness and utilization vary substantially across models. Improvements are concentrated around holidays, where calendar information provides signals unavailable from target history, while some model encoding combinations also improve non-holiday forecasts. A SHAP-based attribution analysis locates the contribution of the covariates relative to the autoregressive component and explains why some model–encoding combinations degrade performance. Our findings suggest that current benchmarks for covariate-informed TSFMs can distort model comparisons by imposing fixed encoding strategies. Future benchmarks should therefore evaluate multiple encodings or provide model-specific encoding strategies aligned with each model’s best practices.

1 Introduction

Accurate time series forecasts are essential for downstream decisions in energy, transport, retail, finance, and other domains, where forecast errors directly affect operational costs. While forecasting has traditionally relied on dataset-specific models that require sufficient historical data and computing power, time series foundation models (TSFMs) have emerged as a compelling alternative (Liang et al., 2024): pretrained on large, heterogeneous datasets, TSFMs can generalize learned temporal patterns to new forecasting tasks without further task-specific training, and have demonstrated impressive performance in benchmarks such as fev-bench (Shchur et al., 2026) or GIFT-Eval (Aksu et al., 2024). Given past observations of the target series, TSFMs can recognize the underlying structure from the context and implicitly activate the parts of the model that are best suited to it when similar series have been observed during pretraining. This zero-shot capability enables high scalability, allowing TSFMs to address forecasting tasks with limited historical data, while their input-driven predictions can improve robustness to distribution shifts. However, relying exclusively on target history has inherent limitations. It is most effective when the series exhibits strong autoregressive structure, but partially fails when the target series is affected by external factors such as public holidays, which recur at irregular intervals and can hardly be inferred from past observations alone. Recent work has therefore begun incorporating calendar information as categorical features into TSFMs with promising results, yet the impact of their encoding on forecast performance remains largely unexplored. This question is particularly relevant for pretrained models, since encoding is one of the few design choices available at inference time, and differences in pretraining strategies may lead to different requirements for representing additional categorical inputs. Furthermore, current benchmarks do not isolate covariate skill or test whether models use informative covariates while ignoring uninformative ones (Meyer et al., 2026a). Our contributions in the present study are as follows:

  • •

    We systematically analyze seven different encoding strategies for calendar information as covariates across four state-of-the-art TSFMs, and evaluate their effect on forecast accuracy on nine diverse datasets from multiple domains, that are influenced by social activities such as weekends and holidays.

  • •

    We employ Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) to examine how models utilize the available covariates and to assess the role of calendar information in forecasting performance.

This study is structured as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on TSFMs with covariate integration, with a particular focus on categorical feature encoding. Section 3 presents the proposed methodology. Section 4 describes the experimental design, while Section 5 and 6 present and discuss the results. Section 7 concludes the work with a summary and outlook.

2 Related Work and Foundations

This section reviews related work on the integration of covariates into TSFMs and encoding strategies for calendar features.

Time Series Foundation Models and Covariates

TSFMs have demonstrated impressive cross-domain performance, often matching or outperforming models trained from scratch (Aksu et al., 2024; Shchur et al., 2026). While early TSFMs, such as Chronos (Ansari et al., 2024) or MOMENT (Goswami et al., 2024), were mostly limited to univariate forecasting, recent models increasingly support the integration of past and future covariates. Two approaches can be distinguished. Adapters such as CoRa (Qin et al., 2025), UniCA (Han et al., 2026) or TFMAdapter (Dange and Sarawagi, 2025) are built on univariate backbones, whereas models like Chronos-2, TabPFN-TS-3 or TiRex-2 offer native covariate support. In studies across different domains such as electrical load forecasting (Hertel et al., 2026a; Kreusel et al., 2026), electricity price forecasting (Pan and Ezzat, 2026), finance (Das et al., 2026) or photovoltaic generation (Longarini et al., 2026), covariate integration has demonstrated performance gains, highlighting the potential of covariate-informed TSFMs and motivating further research in this direction. However, gains are not universal, as Meyer et al. (2026a) report that covariates degrade the performance of t0−b​e​t​at_{0}-beta on 11 of 30 fev-tasks with known-future covariates. Whether these degradations stem from uninformative covariates themselves or from their representation cannot be decided from the reported results.

Covariate Encoding

Covariates in time series forecasting are commonly distinguished into continuous and categorical features (Fahrmeir et al., 2021). While continuous features are already numeric and, depending on the used model, require only standardization or normalization, categorical features must first be mapped to a numeric representation (Hancock and Khoshgoftaar, 2020). For this, multiple encoding methods exist and can broadly be distinguished into target-agnostic and target-based approaches (Pargent et al., 2022; Micci-Barreca, 2001). Target-agnostic methods, such as ordinal, one-hot, or cyclic encoding, derive representations exclusively from the categories themselves, whereas target-based methods additionally incorporate observed target values. In time series forecasting, categorical features are commonly calendar-derived, including temporal features such as hour, weekday, and month, as well as holiday information (Meisenbacher et al., 2022). While the former mainly differ in their temporal granularity, holiday features offer the possibility to further group holidays into different categories. Ziel (2018) compares 31 holiday encoding strategies on German load data, mainly distinguishing fixed-date and weekday-based holidays. Holiday modeling reduces forecast error by >80 % on holidays and about 10 % on ordinary days, while finer grouping is not consistently beneficial. Cho et al. (2013) group holidays by season, Wagner et al. (2022) distinguish federal from regional holidays and introduce bridge days, while Gaillard et al. (2016) additionally classify the days before and after public holidays, capturing their effects on electrical load. In the context of TSFMs, categorical covariates have recently received closer attention, with several studies reporting improved forecast accuracy. Kaas et al. (2026) employ weekday and holiday features, Kreusel et al. (2026) and Hertel et al. (2026a) use holiday features, and Grauer and Ploennigs (2026) use binary indicators for working hours in an office building. While all of the studies rely on different encoding schemes, the encoding itself is treated as an implementation detail rather than as an object of study, and a systematic comparison is missing. However, such a comparison is particularly relevant, as recent benchmarks such as fev-bench (Shchur et al., 2026) and FETS (Obermeier et al., 2026) include covariate-informed tasks with calendar-derived features. In fev-bench, categorical covariates are heterogeneously encoded, with categories stored as float32, string, or boolean. This heterogeneity is consequential, as no task declares a column as categorical and every model wrapper dispatches on the storage dtype alone. FETS sidesteps this problem by storing every covariate numerically: five sine–cosine pairs for the periodic calendar components and binary Int8 indicators for holidays and weekends. While formulating generalizing statements across models is already difficult in the univariate setting due to data leakage (Meyer et al., 2026b), the covariate setting adds further complexity, since each wrapper resolves the encoding differently. No prior work accounts for this additional factor, leaving its effect on TSFM performance unquantified.

3 Methodology

This section introduces the two components used throughout this work. Section 3.1 presents the calendar encodings under study. Section 3.2 introduces the used SHAP approach.

3.1 Calendar Encodings

Table 1 summarizes the calendar encodings applied in this study. We implement several different encodings, based on common approaches in the literature, roughly sorted by increasing complexity to cover most conceivable encoding strategies. All encodings use hour (h), weekday (W), and holiday (H) information, with the indices in the nomenclature indicating how each information is incorporated. The encodings can be divided into two categories. Conventional encodings, comprising ordinal, one-hot, and cyclic encodings, are based exclusively on calendar information and are further enriched with a binary holiday feature to account for the effect of public holidays. Furthermore, we employ simple target encoding strategies that compute the mean target value over the observations in the model context that share the same combination of the incorporated categorical variables, leading to daily profiles on the scale of the target. Mathematically, the target encodings are described as follows: Let 𝒳j\mathcal{X}_{j} denote the set of possible values of the jj-th of kk categorical variables, let xt∈𝒳1×⋯×𝒳kx_{t}\in\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{X}_{k} denote the kk-tuple of categorical values at time step tt, and let x∗∈𝒳1×⋯×𝒳k{x}^{*}\in\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{X}_{k} denote a specific tuple combination. Furthermore, 𝒞=(1,…,c)\mathcal{C}=(1,\ldots,c) indexes the model context and ℱ=(c+1,…,c+f)\mathcal{F}=(c+1,\ldots,c+f) the forecast horizon. For a specific combination x∗{x}^{*} we collect the context time steps that realize it, 𝒵x∗:={t∈𝒞∣xt=x∗}\mathcal{Z}_{{x}^{*}}:=\{t\in\mathcal{C}\mid x_{t}={x}^{*}\}, and define the associated target encoding as the mean target value over this set,

Tx∗=1|𝒵x∗|​∑t∈𝒵x∗Yt,T_{{x}^{*}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Z}_{{x}^{*}}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{Z}_{{x}^{*}}}Y_{t}, (1)

where YtY_{t} denotes the target at time step tt. Every time step t∈𝒞∪ℱt\in\mathcal{C}\cup\mathcal{F} then receives the encoding TxtT_{x_{t}} of its own combination, assuming that each combination that occurs in the horizon occurs at least once within the context. As the encodings are recomputed for every prediction window from the context alone, they introduce no information beyond what the model already receives as input.
Detailed descriptions and visualizations of the encodings are part of Appendix A.1.1.

3.2 SHAP-based Analysis for Identifying Contributions in Forecast

To quantify the contributions of the calendar covariates relative to the past target, we adopt the sampling-free SHAP approach of Hertel et al. (2026a) and extend it from Chronos-2 and TabPFN-TS to TiRex-2 and TimesFM-3. SHAP (Lundberg and Lee, 2017) decomposes a forecast into additive contributions of feature groups 𝒢={g1,…,gM}\mathcal{G}=\{g_{1},\dots,g_{M}\}, given by their Shapley values:

SHAP⁡(gi)=∑S⊆𝒢∖{gi}|S|!​(M−|S|−1)!M!​(f⁡(S∪{gi})−f⁡(S)),\mathrm{SHAP}(g_{i})=\sum_{S\subseteq\mathcal{G}\setminus\{g_{i}\}}\frac{|S|!\,(M-|S|-1)!}{M!}\big(f(S\cup\{g_{i}\})-f(S)\big), (2)

where f⁡(S)f(S) is the forecast given only the groups in coalition SS. SHAP⁡(gi)\mathrm{SHAP}(g_{i}) is thus the average change in the forecast caused by adding gig_{i}, averaged over all coalitions of the other groups. Models with a fixed input dimension cannot evaluate f⁡(S)f(S) with features missing, so model-agnostic estimators such as KernelSHAP (Lundberg and Lee, 2017) replace absent features with samples from background data, which can create unrealistic feature combinations. TSFMs, in contrast, accept arbitrary context lengths and covariate sets, so absent groups can simply be withheld and f⁡(S)f(S) is evaluated directly. Following Hertel et al. (2026a), the past target values are split into four temporal groups, and each covariate forms one additional group. We report the summed contribution of the temporal groups as a single past-target contribution. Details on grouping, masking, and model-specific adaptations are given in Appendix A.1.2.

4 Experimental Setup

Comparing encodings requires an evaluation that isolates the effect of the representation from the effect of the model. We therefore evaluate every encoding on the same datasets, with the same forecast windows, and with the same models. The following paragraphs summarize the models, the datasets, the experiment design, and the metrics. A more detailed description is part of Appendix A.2.

Models

We evaluate four state-of-the-art TSFMs, Chronos-2 (Ansari et al., 2025), TabPFN-TS-3 (Grinsztajn et al., 2026), TiRex-2 (Podest et al., 2026), and TimesFM-3 (Das et al., 2024; Google Research, 2026), alongside two baselines. These are a seasonal naive model with a 168-hour seasonal period and the pure target encoding Th,W​(H=Sun)T_{h,W}(H=\mathrm{Sun}), used without TSFMs and recomputed for each forecast window from the same context used for the TSFMs. For a more detailed description of all models and the model pipeline see Appendix A.2.1.

Datasets

We evaluate nine datasets across the domains energy, transportation, traffic and water. Each dataset provides exactly one year of test data at an hourly resolution. To our knowledge, none of the datasets are included in the pretraining corpora of the employed TSFMs. A detailed list of all datasets is provided in Appendix A.2.2. We enrich each dataset with holiday information derived via the holidays Python library, using its most precise known geographic location.

Evaluation Metrics

For consistency with fev-bench, we evaluate point and probabilistic forecasts using mean absolute scaled error (MASE) (Hyndman and Koehler, 2006) and scaled quantile loss (SQL) (Koenker and Bassett, 1978; Hyndman and Koehler, 2006), as defined in Appendix A.2.3. Both metrics are scaled by the in-sample error of a seasonal-naive forecast with a 168-hour seasonal period, computed separately for each forecast window. Both metrics are implemented using the fev-bench evaluation library (Shchur et al., 2026).

Experiment Design

We evaluate all models in a zero-shot setting, using a rolling evaluation across all datasets and encodings. Since longer context lengths have been shown to improve TSFM performance (Hertel et al., 2026b; Kreusel et al., 2026), we use a context length of 8192, as it is the maximum context length of Chronos-2. Forecast horizon and stride are both set to 24 hours, and each forecast starts at 00:00. To isolate covariate effects, we report holiday and non-holiday results separately.

Hypotheses

Within each model, encoding is the only factor varied across runs, with all other parameters held constant. Since all encodings contain identical calendar information and differ only in representation and covariate count, accuracy differences can be attributed to the encoding. Based on this setup, we formulate three expectations. First, as the four TSFMs differ in their pretraining and in how covariates enter the architecture, we expect the sensitivity to the representation to be model-specific. Second, we expect gains to concentrate around holidays, which, unlike hour and weekday effects, cannot be inferred from the target history. Third, we expect target encodings to be more robust, as they condense target-scale information into one or two covariates, whereas conventional encodings add up to 32 target-agnostic covariates that may dilute the autoregressive signal.

5 Results

Table 2 reports the overall results averaged over the nine datasets, and the per-dataset tables are given in Appendix A.3. As all test sets are equally long and MASE and SQL are scale-independent, no dataset disproportionately influences the overall results. We report results for all days, for holiday windows, and for non-holiday windows, and within a column, the best value across all models and baselines is set in bold and the best value within a model group is underlined. First, we analyze general effects across models, followed by the effects of the encodings within each model.

Overall results across all days

TimesFM-3 achieves the best overall performance on model-level with the cyclich,W + binH encoding, followed by Chronos-2 with the Th,W+Th,HT_{h,W}+T_{h,H} encoding. Relative to the best performance of each model, no general pattern across encodings emerges, as can be seen in the pairwise win rate in Figure 1. While Chronos-2, TabPFN-TS-3, and TiRex-2 perform best with target encodings, TimesFM-3 shows largely comparable performance across encodings, with its best result not obtained by a target encoding.

Results on holidays only

TimesFM-3 achieves the overall best holiday performance with the Th,W​(H=Sun)T_{h,W}(H=\mathrm{Sun}) encoding. On holiday windows covariates improve performance across 26 of the 28 model-encoding combinations, with TiRex-2 using one-hoth,W + binH and cyclich,W + binH encoding as the only exceptions. Across models, target encodings clearly outperform conventional encodings on holidays, indicating that they capture substantially more information than the binary holiday representations of the conventional encodings.

Results on non-holidays only

TimesFM-3 achieves the best model-level performance with the cyclich,W + binH encoding, which explains its overall advantage given that non-holidays constitute the vast majority of days. Encoding effects vary substantially across models, preventing a general conclusion. While Chronos-2, TiRex-2, and TimesFM-3 show only marginal gains or even deteriorations from covariates, TabPFN-TS-3 exhibits a clear improvement in mean forecast accuracy across all encodings.

The findings so far describe general effects across models. In the following, the focus shifts to the different effects of encodings within each model.

Chronos-2 benefits most from two separate target encodings

Chronos-2 reaches its best results on all window types using target encodings, with the Th,W+Th,HT_{h,W}+T_{h,H} encoding. While conventional encodings also improve performance on holidays, they decrease performance on non-holidays (cf. Figure 2), indicating that the target scale representation of calendar information helps the model to capture autoregressive structure within the target series, while the pure calendar information of the conventional encoding dilutes the signal.

TabPFN-TS-3 benefits from every encoding strategy

TabPFN-TS-3 is the only model that improves under all seven encodings and in all three window types. While improvements of target encodings and conventional encodings are on par on holidays, target encodings beat the conventional encodings on non-holidays (cf. Figure 2). Still, conventional encodings improve the non-holiday MASE by up to 5.8 %, indicating that the model relies on additional calendar information even when capturing the autoregressive structure of non-holiday periods.

TiRex-2 can benefit from covariates but is sensitive to multidimensional encodings

Of the seven encodings, only the three joint target encodings improve the mean all-day MASE of TiRex-2. All encodings that comprise two or more covariates show almost no, or a negative effect on the mean performance on both window types, indicating the incapability of the model to handle multiple covariates at once. A noteworthy observation is that TiRex-2 does not show substantial improvements on the mta_subway and mta_bus datasets with any encoding, especially in comparison to the other three models (cf. Appendix A.3.2 and A.3.3, Figures 14 and 16).

TimesFM-3 benefits from covariates only on holidays

On holidays, TimesFM-3 substantially improves over the non-covariate model with all encoding strategies, and target encodings consistently outperform conventional encodings. In contrast, on non-holidays, covariates provide no meaningful improvement over the non-covariate baseline, and all target encodings reduce performance.

6 Discussion

This section discusses generalizable observations across models based on the experiments in Section 5. We use SHAP analyses to provide further insights into the observed effects. Beyond cross-model comparisons, SHAP analyses can also investigate encoding-dependent performance differences within models, helping to identify which encodings work, and in which scenarios they fail.

Encodings substantially impact performance across all models and data regimes

The results demonstrate that the choice of encoding substantially affects model performance across all models, with effects differing between holidays and non-holidays. While the gap in MASE between the best and worst encoding within a model ranges from +4.8 % (TiRex-2) to +9.9 % (TabPFN-TS-3) on non-holidays, the gap is between +44 % (TabPFN-TS-3) to +83 % (TiRex-2) on holidays. The large differences between holidays and non-holidays can be explained by the SHAP contributions shown in Figure 3, illustrated for the Th,W​(H=7)T_{h,W}(H=7) and Th,W+Th,HT_{h,W}+T_{h,H} encodings. On holidays, all models assign substantially greater importance to the calendar features than on non-holidays. On non-holidays, Chronos-2 is less influenced by either of the two encodings than the other models, instead relying primarily on the autoregressive structure of the series, explaining the only marginally changed performance compared to its non-covariate variant. In contrast, TimesFM-3 places more weight on the calendar features than Chronos-2, yet performs worse than its own non-covariate variant under both depicted encodings. This indicates that the model already captures the underlying autoregressive structure effectively, and that the covariate information dilutes the signal.

Encoding effectiveness and utilization vary across models

While encoding choice affects performance across all models, the effects of specific encodings do not generalize across them. Figure 4 illustrates this exemplarily for a holiday and a non-holiday of the m_dense dataset with the Th,W+Th,HT_{h,W}+T_{h,H} encoding. While Chronos-2, TabPFN-TS-3, and TimesFM-3 on holidays correctly assign more weight to the holiday covariate Th,HT_{h,H} than the weekday and hour information Th,WT_{h,W}, the two covariate effects nearly cancel out for TiRex-2, producing an overestimated forecast. Such differences in how models handle specific encoding strategies likely stem from architectural and training differences. Chronos-2, for instance, applies target encoding during training but specifies neither which features are included nor whether their granularity adapts to the target frequency.

Encodings in the context of benchmarking

The strong influence of encoding choice on model performance, combined with its varying effects across models, has direct implications for multivariate benchmarking. Current benchmarks such as FETS (Obermeier et al., 2026) and fev-bench (Shchur et al., 2026) evaluate all models under a single fixed encoding, determined by data type of the dataset. Their conclusions are therefore limited to the specific model–encoding combinations tested and cannot be generalized to the full potential of a model, as alternative encodings may change the observed ranking. This can for example be observed in a second experimental run with context length 2048 (cf. Appendix A.3.11). Two complementary remedies are possible. Benchmarks could include multiple encoding strategies as an explicit evaluation factor, allowing each model to be assessed across different preprocessing choices rather than under a single fixed encoding. Alternatively, model developers could integrate model-specific categorical feature handling directly into the model, for example by accepting ordinal inputs and applying the internally optimal transformation, or publish a best-practice encoding recommendation against which their model should be evaluated. Both approaches shift the object of evaluation from the performance of a particular encoding to the actual potential of a model in multivariate forecasting.

Limitations

All experiments use context length 8192, the maximum of Chronos-2, corresponding to roughly 49 weeks at hourly resolution. A second run with context 2048 (cf. Appendix A.3.11) confirms our findings, but a context exceeding one year is of interest, as human behavior often follows an annual cycle that would then be fully contained in the context. Furthermore, all datasets are evaluated at hourly resolution, and additional resolutions would further validate the results. Finally, our study is restricted to settings where the target follows calendar effects such as holidays and weekends. For problems driven mainly by continuous exogenous drivers such as solar irradiance or temperature, no comparable benefit is expected. Incorporating such covariates is left to future work.

7 Summary and Outlook

Although covariates are increasingly used with TSFMs, their encoding is typically treated as an implementation detail rather than systematically investigated. Existing multivariate benchmarks commonly fix a single encoding across models and datasets, potentially conflating model capability with encoding choice. To demonstrate this, we systematically evaluate multiple calendar encodings across different TSFMs and datasets. Our results can be summarized in three key findings:

  • •

    Encodings impact performance across all models and data regimes.

  • •

    The effectiveness and utilization of specific encodings varies across models, indicating a strong interaction between model architecture and representation.

  • •

    Encoding effects should be considered in future multivariate benchmarks, as fixing a single encoding can influence and potentially distort model rankings.

Future work should revisit existing benchmarks by treating encoding as an explicit experimental factor. Beyond evaluation, our results suggest that improved encoding strategies offer an opportunity for future research. A promising direction is a fully data-driven approach, such as in-context clustering, where time-series-specific characteristics are identified from the context and used to derive or select suitable encodings. This could enable more adaptive representations of covariate information and lead to further improved TSFM forecasting performance.

Reproducibility Statement

All code required to reproduce our results will be made publicly available upon publication, including the evaluation pipeline, and the scripts that generate every table and figure. All experiments use publicly available benchmark data.

Appendix A Appendix

This section provides further information on our methodology, experimental design and the results. It is structured as follows: Section A.1.1 explains and visualizes all encoding strategies, and provides further details on the applied SHAP method. Section A.2 contains detailed information on the datasets, models, evaluation metrics, and the hardware and software used in this study. Section A.3 contains the dataset specific results of the experiments of the main part of the study, as well as the results of a second experiment run with context length 2048.

A.1 Methodology

A.1.1 Encodings

ordinalh,W + binH

The ordinalh,W + binH encoding represents hours using values from 0 to 23 and weekdays using values from 0 to 6. Holidays are binary encoded, resulting in three covariates in total. Figure 5 illustrates all three covariates and their behavior during weekdays and holidays.

one-hoth,W + binH

The one-hoth,W + binH encoding represents hour and weekday using a one-hot encoding. Holidays are binary encoded, resulting in 32 covariates in total. Figure 6 illustrates all 32 covariates and their behavior during weekdays and holidays.

cyclich,W + binH

The cyclich,W + binH encoding represents hour and weekday using sine and cosine functions, while holidays are binary encoded, resulting in five covariates in total. Figure 7 illustrates all five covariates and their behavior on holidays. This encoding strategy is very similar to the fixed encoding applied in the FETS benchmark (Obermeier et al., 2026), where minute, hour, weekday, day, and month are encoded with sine and cosine functions, and holidays are encoded binary.

Th,W​(H=Sun)T_{h,W}(H=\mathrm{Sun})

The Th,W​(H=Sun)T_{h,W}(H=\mathrm{Sun}) encoding is a target encoding with the categories hour (0–23) and weekday (0–6), where holidays are mapped to Sunday. Accordingly, the resulting encoding for Sundays and holidays in Figure 8 is identical.

Th,W​(H=7)T_{h,W}(H=7)

The Th,W​(H=7)T_{h,W}(H=7) encoding is a target encoding with the categories hour and weekday. While hour is encoded as 0–23, as in Th,W​(H=Sun)T_{h,W}(H=\mathrm{Sun}), holidays are treated as a separate weekday category, so weekday is encoded as 0 to 7. Accordingly, different encoding profiles are formed for Sundays and holidays, as can be seen in Figure 9.

Th,W,HT_{h,W,H}

The Th,W,HT_{h,W,H} encoding (cf. Figure 10) is a target encoding with the categories hour (0–23), weekday (0–6), and holiday (0 or 1). Treating holidays as a separate category leads to separate holiday encoding profiles for each weekday, e.g., the encoding for a holiday that falls on a Monday is exclusively calculated from past holidays that also fell on a Monday. This target encoding can potentially suffer from data scarcity, since a given weekday–holiday combination may occur only a few times, or not at all in the context.

Th,W+Th,HT_{h,W}+T_{h,H}

The Th,W+Th,HT_{h,W}+T_{h,H} encoding consists of two separate target encodings, both of which are used as model inputs. Th,WT_{h,W} uses the categories hour (0–23) and weekday (0–6), while Th,HT_{h,H} uses the categories hour (0–23) and holiday (0 or 1). Figure 11 shows the resulting encodings. By combining both covariates, the Th,W+Th,HT_{h,W}+T_{h,H} encoding contains the same weekday and holiday information as all the other encoding strategies.

A.1.2 SHAP Methodology

SHAP values are computed for the Th,W​(H=7)T_{h,W}(H{=}7) and Th,W+Th,HT_{h,W}+T_{h,H} encodings, for the median point forecast of each horizon step and forecast window. Figure 4 shows these per-step values. Figure 3 reports mean absolute SHAP values averaged over horizon steps, forecast windows, and datasets, separately for holidays and non-holidays. For the SHAP analyses, we directly call the native model APIs, bypassing fev.ForecastingModel to enable feature-subset masking.

Feature groups

As in Hertel et al. (2026a), the past target is split into four temporal groups. Together with the covariate groups, this yields M=5M=5 groups for Th,W​(H=7)T_{h,W}(H{=}7) and M=6M=6 for Th,W+Th,HT_{h,W}+T_{h,H}. All 2M2^{M} coalitions, i.e., 32 or 64 per forecast, are evaluated, so we obtain exact SHAP values. For clarity, the figures show the summed contribution of the temporal groups, which reduces them to two or three groups.

Masking

For each coalition, the context starts at the earliest active temporal group, inactive target values are set to NaN, and inactive covariates are removed. Without any active temporal group, the context mean serves as the base prediction f⁡(∅)f(\emptyset). The target encodings are computed once from the full context and are not recomputed under masking. Their Shapley values therefore capture the full contribution of the encoding as provided to the model, including the target statistics it summarizes. This is the quantity of interest, as it shows to what extent a model relies on the encoded calendar profile instead of the past target values.

Model-specific masking

Chronos-2 and TabPFN-TS-3 are handled as in Hertel et al. (2026a). Since TiRex-2 also handles NaN values natively, it is treated in the same way as Chronos-2. TimesFM-3 would fill NaN values with zeros or interpolate across them, which leaks masked information. We therefore pass the masked positions to its internal target mask.

A.2 Experimental Setup

A.2.1 Models and Pipeline

Chronos-2

(Ansari et al., 2025) is a 120M-parameter TSFM based on an encoder-only Transformer architecture. It is pretrained on large-scale real and synthetic time-series data and models temporal and cross-series dependencies through temporal and group attention. It produces multi-step quantile forecasts, with the median used as point forecast.

TabPFN-TS-3

(Grinsztajn et al., 2026) is a 58M-parameter checkpoint of TabPFN-3, trained exclusively on synthetic data. Following Hoo et al. (2026), it represents each time step as a row of temporal features, with optional future known covariates. It predicts the full forecast horizon in a single pass, outputting a discretized predictive distribution from which quantiles are derived, with the median used as point forecast.

TiRex-2

(Podest et al., 2026) is an 82M-parameter TSFM based on a recurrent xLSTM architecture that extends TiRex (Auer et al., 2025) to multivariate targets with past and future known covariates. It is pretrained on real and synthetic univariate data and models temporal and cross-variate dependencies through alternating time and variate mixing blocks. It produces multi-step quantile forecasts, with the median used as point forecast.

TimesFM-3

(Google Research, 2026) is a 330M-parameter TSFM based on a decoder-only transformer architecture that supports multivariate targets with past and future known covariates. It is pretrained on a corpus of real and synthetic time series comprising more than 1T time points. Inputs are split into patches of 32 time steps, and future known covariates use lookahead tokens that concatenate the current patch with future patches. The model captures temporal and cross-variate dependencies through alternating causal time attention and full variate attention layers. The model predicts the full forecast horizon in a single pass and outputs quantiles, with the median used as point forecast.

Baseline Models

We use two baseline models to assess the forecasting performance of the TSFMs. The first is a non-holiday-aware seasonal naive model with a seasonal period of 168 hours. The second is the target encoding Th,W​(H=Sun)T_{h,W}(H=\mathrm{Sun}) itself (cf. Table 1), recomputed for each forecast window based on a context of 8192 observations. Both baselines produce quantile forecasts as a Gaussian band around their point forecast, whose width is given by the standard deviation of residuals over all context timesteps. For the seasonal naive model, these are the residuals of each observation against the observation exactly one season (168 hours) earlier. For the target-encoding baseline, they are the residuals of each observation against its timestep-matched encoding value, pooled across all day-type/hour cells present in the context.

Pipeline

All covariates are provided in numeric form (int64 or float64) as fev-dataset. No column is passed as a string, boolean or categorical dtype, so no model applies a dtype-triggered encoding of its own. To the best of the authors knowledge, two models nevertheless branch on the covariate values: TabPFN-TS-3 infers categorical features from cardinality and re-encodes them internally, and the TiRex-2 checkpoint used here detects binary variates and bypasses its instance scaling for them. Both branches are triggered by exactly the binary indicator columns, i.e. the one-hot encoding and the binary holiday flags; the ordinal, cyclic and target encodings are unaffected in all four models.

A.2.2 Datasets

Table 3 summarizes all datasets used in this study. The test period of each dataset spans exactly one year. While the m_dense, mta_subway and mta_bus datasets natively have an hourly resolution, the TransnetBW and FeederBW sets originally have higher frequencies and are resampled to hourly resolution using the mean. From the FeederBW dataset, the three selected series are evaluated separately and referred to as FeederBW_33, FeederBW_35, and FeederBW_91. None of the datasets used in this study are included in the pretraining corpora of the employed TSFMs, excluding train-test leakage (Meyer et al., 2026b). We evaluate all models in zero-shot setting, using a rolling evaluation across all datasets and encoding strategies.

A.2.3 Evaluation Metrics

MASE and SQL are implemented in the fev-bench evaluation library (Shchur et al., 2026), but are outlined here consistent with our notation.

Mean Absolute Scaled Error
MASE=1N​∑i=1N(1f​∑h=1f|Yi,c+h−Y^i,c+h|1c−m​∑s=m+1c|Yi,s−Yi,s−m|).\operatorname{MASE}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\frac{\dfrac{1}{f}\sum_{h=1}^{f}\left|Y_{i,c+h}-\hat{Y}_{i,c+h}\right|}{\dfrac{1}{c-m}\sum_{s=m+1}^{c}\left|Y_{i,s}-Y_{i,s-m}\right|}\right). (3)

The mean absolute scaled error (MASE) is a point forecast metric that scales forecast errors by the in-sample MAE of a seasonal naïve forecast, making it scale-independent. MASE is defined as in Equation 3, where NN denotes the number of prediction windows, ff the length of the forecast horizon ℱ=(c+1,…,c+f)\mathcal{F}=(c+1,\ldots,c+f), Yi,c+hY_{i,c+h} the observed value at forecast step h∈{1,…,f}h\in\{1,\ldots,f\} of prediction window ii, and Y^i,c+h\hat{Y}_{i,c+h} the corresponding forecast. Furthermore, cc denotes the length of the context window 𝒞=(1,…,c)\mathcal{C}=(1,\ldots,c), mm the seasonal period, and Yi,sY_{i,s} the observed value at context position s∈𝒞s\in\mathcal{C} of window ii. In this study, the seasonal period is set to m=168m=168 hours, and the seasonal error is re-computed for each context window (Hyndman and Koehler, 2006).

Scaled Quantile Loss
SQL=1N​∑i=1N(1|𝒬|​f​∑τ∈𝒬∑h=1fρτ​(Yi,c+h−Y^i,c+h(τ))1c−m​∑s=m+1c|Yi,s−Yi,s−m|).\operatorname{SQL}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\frac{\dfrac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|\,f}\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{Q}}\sum_{h=1}^{f}\rho_{\tau}\!\left(Y_{i,c+h}-\hat{Y}_{i,c+h}^{(\tau)}\right)}{\dfrac{1}{c-m}\sum_{s=m+1}^{c}\left|Y_{i,s}-Y_{i,s-m}\right|}\right). (4)

We report the scaled quantile loss (SQL), which averages the pinball loss (Koenker and Bassett, 1978) over the quantile grid 𝒬={0.1,0.2,…,0.9}\mathcal{Q}=\{0.1,0.2,\ldots,0.9\} and scales it by the in-sample seasonal-naive error (Hyndman and Koehler, 2006), making it the probabilistic extension of MASE. SQL is defined as in Equation 4, where ρτ\rho_{\tau} denotes the pinball loss at quantile level τ\tau. As for MASE, we use a seasonal period of m=168m=168 hours, and the seasonal-naive error is computed separately for each context window.

A.2.4 Hardware and Software

Compute environment.

All experiments were run on a single workstation with one NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU. The benchmark is implemented in Python 3.11.15 on top of the fev 0.10.0 evaluation framework; all models are wrapped as fev.ForecastingModel implementations so that data loading, window construction (fixed context of 8192 hourly steps for every model, horizon 24, stride 24) and metric computation are identical across models. The foundation models run on the single GPU using PyTorch 2.9.1; the naive baselines are CPU-only. No distributed execution is used.

A.3.10 Overall Results with Ground Truth as Covariate

Table 13 shows a setting in which the ground-truth target is provided as a known covariate. The results therefore represent the maximum performance each model can reach by exploiting covariate information. TabPFN-TS-3 and TimesFM-3 nearly reproduce the target. Chronos-2 and TiRex-2 remain at a MASE of about 0.30 despite perfect information, and Chronos-2 performs notably worse on holidays. The benefit of holiday covariates is thus limited not only by the information they contain but also by each model’s ability to use it.
